title_content.content: What we've learned about HDDs over the last 3 weeks during our Taiwan AI Summit, COMPUTEX, and WDC Asia Roadshow. A few very important, new datapoints:

item_content.content: - Demand is strengthening. We are now hearing that nearline HDD supply will be 300EB's short of demand in CY26 (10-15% shortage), 400EB's short of demand in CY27, and 400EB's short of demand in CY28. Why? Core cloud services growth is outperforming and AI inferencing/agents are driving upside to general-purpose server shipments and HDD demand. For reference, we are hearing hyperscalers are deploying HDDs at close to a 100% rate vs. ~70% historically, suggesting limited inventory build at CSPs. Further, HDD inventory at ODMs is only 1-2 weeks currently. Overall, we believe HDD demand is growing closer to 40-50% annually, while supply growth is closer to 30-35%.

- HDD pricing is strongly biased upwards. Today, STX's and WDC's blended nearline price per TB is $14.30-14.90. In April, we learned HDD vendors could capture $20/TB for nearline capacity in CY27/CY28. During our time in Taiwan this month, we learned that HDD vendors are targeting up to $25-30/TB for blended nearline pricing in CY27/CY28 (targeting, not already negotiated... we want to be clear). Furthermore, current *spot* HDD prices (i.e., what is charged for customers not on LTAs) are ~30% higher than previously captured, with some distributors selling HDDs for up to $30-35/TB today. It's our understanding that pricing changes for hyperscalers are still communicated well in advance, and typically captured through prescriptive Q/Q pricing escalators within contracts.

- HDD vendors are limiting their use of 12+ month LTAs to capture more favorable commercial terms. While hyperscalers are asking for LTAs out to 2032, HDD vendors are less willing to sign deals this long. Why? Because applications for HDDs / cold storage are broadening, shortages are growing, the TCO vs. NAND is significantly improving, and HDD replacement technology remains non-existent. To be clear, STX/WDC want to provide their customers with 5 years of visibility on capacity and technology introductions, but are just less eager to attach commercial terms 12+ months out.

paragraph_content.content: We want to put some of these pricing data points in context. We, by no means, want to minimize checks that point to a strengthening HDD demand environment. But the HDD vendors are very disciplined on supply (i.e., no greenfield capacity buildouts), and thus nearline EB growth over the next 2-3 years will be dictated by supply, which we believe is growing at a 30-35% CAGR. Conversely, we want to be very clear on exactly how impactful these pricing checks could be to STX/WDC's financial model. This is because any incremental pricing upside is effectively all profit (tax effected). As seen in Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 below, if we were to assume blended nearline price per TB reached $25 in CY27 and $30 in CY28 – in line with our Taiwan checks – STX could generate >$70 of EPS in CY27 and >$100 of EPS in CY28, while WDC could do >$40 of EPS in CY27 and >$70 of EPS in CY28. For reference, STX/WDC did $10.24 / $6.95 of EPS in CY25, implying a 10x-ing of EPS over 3 years. To be clear, we don't want to imply this is the market base case today – our new CY27 STX base case EPS is $51, while our CY27 WDC base case EPS if $32. But if these checks prove accurate, our bull case valuations of ~$1,446 for STX and $920 for WDC are clearly in play.

paragraph_content.content: Furthermore, HDDs are in the midst of a 10-year technology transition, and the risk of new entrants is limited, in our conversations. Outside of a reversal in cloud capex – which is a risk much broader than HDDs – the most significant risk to our HDD forecasts would be a new entrant that disrupts the powerful, rational HDD oligopoly. During our time with WDC management last week, CEO Irving Tan contextualized this risk for us, explaining that the challenges with becoming competitive as a new entrant are not about capital, but rather: (1) the time it takes to move to the next generation leading-edge node – it's taken over 10 years to qualify HAMR; (2) the ability to internalize/vertically integrate technology across disparate fields of knowledge such as magnetics, material science, photonics, nanofabrication, etc.; and (3) a lack of broad supply chain capacity – the HDD supply chain is very consolidated with limited under-utilization today. Mr. Tan noted Chinese players have tried to create cold-storage alternatives recently (Huawei's Magneto-Electric Disk, for example) but found little success. Overall, we feel comfortable with this risk today.

How our estimates and PTs are changing. With this report, we are only making one significant change in our STX/WDC models – adjusting nearline price per TB higher. We don't make any material changes to EB growth, annual cost declines, or opex. But with modest pricing upside (10-20% higher price/TB in 2027-2028), we now forecast stronger revenue growth, higher gross/operating margins, and stronger buybacks. We also tweak each model for recent convertible debt exchanges. For STX, this means our FY26 EPS doesn't change, but our FY27 EPS increases 11% to $35.38 (from $31.75) and our FY28 EPS increases 30% to $70.64 (from $53.95). Subsequently, this drives our PT to $1,035 (from $767) or 20x CY27 EPS of $51.67, and our bull case valuation to $1,446 (22x bull case CY27 EPS of $65.74). For WDC, our FY26 EPS is also unchanged, while our FY27 EPS increases 13% to $22.40 (from $19.89) and our FY28 EPS increases 25% to $43.47 (from $34.87). Our PT is now $650 (from $488) or 20x CY27 EPS of $32.29, and our bull case valuation is now $920 (22x bull case CY27 EPS of $41.80).

paragraph_content.content: Our latest views on STX vs. WDC. We are Overweight both stocks and see them as our most-preferred OWs within our IT Hardware coverage. That said, we have a tactical bias towards STX, as we see: (1) the ability to re-price early HAMR customers in the September '26 quarter; and (2) the ability to cost down slightly faster than WDC in C2H26 given a higher cost/TB starting point as creating more material gross margin tailwinds for STX vs. WDC over the next 3-6 months. This is why STX is our current 'Top Pick'. However, on a longer-term basis, WDC screens as modestly more attractive given: (1) greater relative upside to our bull case valuation; and (2) a slightly less-levered balance sheet. In reality, we believe clients would benefit from exposure to each stock.
What are the most notable risks to owning HDDs at this point? The key risks to

HDDs remain: (1) the durability and magnitude of this cycle; and (2) the potential for new entrants. On the former, our Asia checks give us comfort in HDD utilization/ customer inventory, and the broadening of demand + growing supply shortages suggest there is durability to this cycle. On the latter, as we discussed above, we see limited risk of new entrants to the HDD market, and/or of a strategic consortium propping up the distant 3rd player in HDDs. However, these remain the two areas we continue to track most closely as we constantly stress-test our theses.
